title: General Random Variables
source: Dimitri P. Bertsekas and John N. Tsitsiklis, Introduction to Probability, MIT course 6.041–6.431, Fall 2000 lecture notes

steps.title: Notation
steps.objective: Read the symbols used for densities, distribution functions, the normal law, joint models, and conditioning.

steps.title: Continuous random variables and PDFs
steps.objective: Recognise what a PDF is, what it is not, and how areas under it give probabilities.

steps.title: Expectation and the exponential
steps.objective: Compute means, variances, and the properties of the exponential random variable.

steps.title: Cumulative distribution functions
steps.objective: Use the CDF to describe discrete and continuous random variables alike.

steps.title: Normal random variables
steps.objective: Standardize a normal random variable and read probabilities from the normal table.

steps.title: Conditioning on an event
steps.objective: Condition a PDF on an event and apply the total probability and total expectation theorems.

steps.title: Multiple continuous random variables
steps.objective: Work with joint, marginal and conditional PDFs, the continuous Bayes rule, and independence.

steps.title: Derived distributions
steps.objective: Find the PDF of a function of one or two random variables.

questions.question: f_X(x)
options: The probability density function of X
The probability that X equals x
The cumulative probability up to x
questions.correct_answer: The probability density function of X
questions.explanation: A PDF is a density: only its area over a set is a probability.

questions.question: ∫_B f_X(x) dx
options: The mean of X over B
questions.correct_answer: P(X ∈ B)
questions.explanation: Integrating the PDF over a set gives the probability of that set.

questions.question: F_X(x)
options: The density of X at x
questions.correct_answer: P(X ≤ x)
questions.explanation: The CDF accumulates probability up to the value x.

questions.question: Φ(y)
options: The PDF of the standard normal random variable
The mean of a normal random variable
The variance of a normal random variable
The CDF of the standard normal random variable
questions.correct_answer: The CDF of the standard normal random variable
questions.explanation: Φ is reserved for the standard normal CDF, the function recorded in the normal table.

questions.question: μ in the normal PDF
options: The mean of the random variable
questions.correct_answer: The mean of the random variable
questions.explanation: The normal PDF is symmetric around μ, which is therefore its mean.

questions.question: σ² in the normal PDF
options: The variance of the random variable
questions.correct_answer: The variance of the random variable
questions.explanation: σ is the standard deviation, so σ² is the variance.

questions.question: λ in the PDF λe^(−λx)
options: The mean of the random variable
The variance of the random variable
The positive parameter of an exponential random variable
questions.correct_answer: The positive parameter of an exponential random variable
questions.explanation: The exponential parameter λ is positive; the mean is 1/λ, not λ.

questions.question: δ in P([x, x+δ]) ≈ f_X(x)·δ
options: The length of a small interval
questions.correct_answer: The length of a small interval
questions.explanation: δ is an interval length taken small, which is why the approximation is good.

questions.question: f_{X,Y}(x,y)
options: The joint PDF of X and Y
The conditional PDF of X given Y
The joint CDF of X and Y
questions.correct_answer: The joint PDF of X and Y
questions.explanation: A joint PDF is integrated over a region of the plane to give a probability.

questions.question: f_{X|Y}(x | y)
options: The joint PDF of X and Y
The conditional PDF of X given that Y = y
The probability that X = x given Y = y
questions.correct_answer: The conditional PDF of X given that Y = y
questions.explanation: It is the joint PDF along the slice Y = y, renormalized to integrate to 1.

questions.question: f_{X|A}(x)
options: The PDF of the event A
The probability of A given X = x
The conditional PDF of X given the event A
The joint PDF of X and A
questions.correct_answer: The conditional PDF of X given the event A
questions.explanation: Conditioning on an event gives an ordinary PDF in a universe where A has occurred.

questions.question: E[X | A]
options: The variance of X given A
The conditional PDF of X given A
The conditional expectation of X given the event A
questions.correct_answer: The conditional expectation of X given the event A
questions.explanation: It integrates x against the conditional PDF f_{X|A}.

questions.question: var(X)
options: The expected value of X − E[X]
The square root of the mean
questions.correct_answer: The expected value of (X − E[X])²
questions.explanation: Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean.

questions.question: The dx in ∫ f_X(x) dx
options: It names the variable the integration runs over
It is the derivative of x
It is a constant multiplying the integral
questions.correct_answer: It names the variable the integration runs over
questions.explanation: The differential marks which variable is being integrated, not a quantity of its own.

questions.question: h in "y = g(x) if and only if x = h(y)"
options: The inverse of the function g
questions.correct_answer: The inverse of the function g
questions.explanation: A strictly monotonic g can be inverted, and h is that inverse.

questions.question: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f_{X,Y}(x,y) dy
options: The conditional PDF of X given Y
questions.correct_answer: The marginal PDF f_X(x)
questions.explanation: Integrating the joint PDF over the other variable leaves the marginal PDF.

questions.question: What makes a random variable X continuous?
options: Its probability law is described by a nonnegative function f_X whose integral over a set gives the probability of that set
questions.correct_answer: Its probability law is described by a nonnegative function f_X whose integral over a set gives the probability of that set
questions.explanation: Continuity is defined by the existence of a PDF, not merely by having many values.

questions.question: For a continuous random variable X and any single value a, P(X = a) equals
questions.explanation: The integral of the PDF over a single point is zero, so including or excluding endpoints changes nothing.

questions.question: Which condition must every PDF satisfy?
options: f_X(x) ≥ 0 for all x and ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f_X(x) dx = 1
The sum of f_X over all x is 1
questions.correct_answer: f_X(x) ≥ 0 for all x and ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f_X(x) dx = 1
questions.explanation: A PDF must be nonnegative and enclose total area one; it is not bounded by one.

questions.question: How should f_X(x) be interpreted?
options: As the probability that X equals x
As the probability that X is at most x
As the average value of X near x
As probability mass per unit length near x
questions.correct_answer: As probability mass per unit length near x
questions.explanation: For small δ, P([x, x+δ]) ≈ f_X(x)·δ, so f_X is a density per unit length.

questions.question: Can a PDF take values larger than 1?
options: Yes, provided the total area under it is still 1
No, a PDF is a probability
Only on intervals of length greater than 1
questions.correct_answer: Yes, provided the total area under it is still 1
questions.explanation: The PDF of Example 3.3 grows without bound near zero and is still legitimate.

questions.question: For a uniform random variable on [a,b], the constant value of the PDF is
questions.explanation: The area of the rectangle of height c over [a,b] is c(b − a), which must equal one.

questions.question: For X uniform on [a,b] and a set I, P(X ∈ I) equals
options: length of I divided by length of [a,b]
length of [a,b] ∩ I divided by length of [a,b]
questions.correct_answer: length of [a,b] ∩ I divided by length of [a,b]
questions.explanation: Only the part of I inside [a,b] carries probability, measured as a fraction of the whole interval.

questions.question: For a piecewise constant PDF with values c_i on [a_i, a_{i+1}), normalization requires
questions.explanation: Each piece contributes the area of its rectangle, and the areas must add to one.

questions.question: The expected value of a continuous random variable X is defined as
options: the value x where f_X is largest
questions.explanation: The discrete sum is replaced by an integral of x against the density.

questions.question: The expected value rule for Y = g(X) states that E[g(X)] equals
questions.explanation: The PDF of Y is not needed: integrate g against the PDF of X.

questions.question: Which identity gives the variance from moments?
questions.correct_answer: var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])²
questions.explanation: Expanding (X − E[X])² and using linearity gives the second moment minus the squared mean.

questions.question: For Y = aX + b with scalars a and b
options: E[Y] = aE[X] + b and var(Y) = a²var(X) + b
E[Y] = E[X] + b and var(Y) = var(X)
E[Y] = aE[X] + b and var(Y) = a²var(X)
questions.correct_answer: E[Y] = aE[X] + b and var(Y) = a²var(X)
questions.explanation: Shifting moves the mean but not the spread; scaling multiplies the variance by a².

questions.question: For X uniform on [a,b], the mean and variance are
questions.correct_answer: (a + b)/2 and (b − a)²/12
questions.explanation: Symmetry gives the midpoint as mean; the second moment (a² + ab + b²)/3 gives the variance.

questions.question: The PDF of an exponential random variable with parameter λ is
questions.correct_answer: λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise
questions.explanation: The factor λ is what makes the area over [0, ∞) equal to one.

questions.question: For an exponential random variable and any a ≥ 0, P(X ≥ a) equals
questions.correct_answer: e^(−λa)
questions.explanation: The tail probability falls exponentially, which is the integral of λe^(−λx) from a to infinity.

questions.question: The mean and variance of an exponential random variable with parameter λ are
questions.correct_answer: 1/λ and 1/λ²
questions.explanation: Integration by parts gives E[X] = 1/λ and E[X²] = 2/λ², leaving variance 1/λ².

questions.question: Why is the CDF defined for every kind of random variable?
options: Because {X ≤ x} is always an event and so always has a probability
Because every random variable has a PDF
Because every random variable has a PMF
Because every random variable is continuous
questions.correct_answer: Because {X ≤ x} is always an event and so always has a probability
questions.explanation: The CDF needs only that {X ≤ x} be an event, which holds discrete or continuous.

questions.question: The CDF of a discrete random variable
options: has a staircase form, jumping at the values of positive probability mass
questions.correct_answer: has a staircase form, jumping at the values of positive probability mass
questions.explanation: Each jump equals the probability mass at that value, and the CDF is continuous from the right.

questions.question: For an integer-valued discrete random variable, the PMF is recovered from the CDF by
questions.correct_answer: p_X(k) = F_X(k) − F_X(k − 1)
questions.explanation: Differencing the accumulated probability leaves the mass at k.

questions.question: For a continuous random variable, the PDF is recovered from the CDF by
questions.correct_answer: differentiating: f_X(x) = dF_X/dx
questions.explanation: Integration builds the CDF from the PDF, so differentiation reverses it wherever the derivative exists.

questions.question: Which pair of properties does every CDF have?
options: It is monotonically nondecreasing, and tends to 0 as x → −∞ and to 1 as x → ∞
It is strictly increasing and bounded by 1/2
It is nonincreasing and tends to 0 at both ends
It is symmetric about its mean
questions.correct_answer: It is monotonically nondecreasing, and tends to 0 as x → −∞ and to 1 as x → ∞
questions.explanation: Accumulating probability can never decrease, and the total accumulated is one.

questions.question: The CDF of an exponential random variable with parameter λ, for x > 0, is
questions.explanation: Integrating λe^(−λt) from 0 to x gives 1 − e^(−λx).

questions.question: The CDF of a geometric random variable with parameter p, at n = 1, 2, …, is
questions.explanation: The geometric series for the first n masses sums to 1 − (1 − p)^n.

questions.question: For the maximum X of three independent scores, each uniform on 1…10, F_X(k) equals
questions.explanation: All three scores must be at most k, and independence multiplies the three probabilities.

questions.question: The PDF of a normal random variable with parameters μ and σ is
questions.explanation: The squared deviation in the exponent is what produces the bell shape around μ.

questions.question: For a normal random variable with parameters μ and σ
questions.correct_answer: E[X] = μ and var(X) = σ²
questions.explanation: Symmetry gives the mean; a change of variables and integration by parts give the variance.

questions.question: If X is normal and Y = aX + b, then Y is
options: normal, with mean μ + b and variance σ²
normal, with mean aμ + b and variance a²σ²
questions.correct_answer: normal, with mean aμ + b and variance a²σ²
questions.explanation: Normality is preserved by linear transformations, which is why standardizing works.

questions.question: A standard normal random variable is one with
questions.correct_answer: zero mean and unit variance
questions.explanation: Its CDF is denoted Φ and is the function tabulated in the normal table.

questions.question: To standardize a normal random variable X with mean μ and variance σ², set Y equal to
questions.correct_answer: (X − μ)/σ
questions.explanation: Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation gives mean 0 and variance 1.

questions.question: Because the standard normal table lists Φ(y) only for y ≥ 0, Φ(−0.5) is found as
questions.explanation: Symmetry of the PDF around zero turns a left tail into the complementary right tail.

questions.question: For X normal with mean μ and variance σ², P(X ≤ x) equals
questions.correct_answer: Φ((x − μ)/σ)
questions.explanation: Standardize both sides of the inequality, then read the standard normal table.

questions.question: Annual snowfall is normal with μ = 60 and σ = 20 inches. Using Φ(1) = 0.8413, P(X ≥ 80) is
questions.explanation: Standardizing gives P(Y ≥ 1) = 1 − Φ(1) = 0.1587.

questions.question: Why does the normal distribution appear in so many models?
options: The sum of many independent, identically distributed random variables has an approximately normal CDF
Every random variable is normal in the limit of small samples
It is the only PDF that integrates to one
Products of independent random variables are normal
questions.correct_answer: The sum of many independent, identically distributed random variables has an approximately normal CDF
questions.explanation: This is the central limit theorem, which makes the normal a good model for additive effects.

questions.question: In the signal detection example with zero-mean noise of variance σ², the probability of error is
questions.explanation: An error needs the noise to cross the distance 1, and both transmitted signals give the same probability by symmetry.

questions.question: Conditioned on the event {X ∈ A} with P(X ∈ A) > 0, the conditional PDF is
options: f_X(x)·P(X ∈ A) for x in A, and 0 otherwise
f_X(x) for x in A, and 0 otherwise
f_X(x)/P(X ∈ A) for x in A, and 0 otherwise
P(X ∈ A) for x in A, and 0 otherwise
questions.correct_answer: f_X(x)/P(X ∈ A) for x in A, and 0 otherwise
questions.explanation: Dividing by P(X ∈ A) is what makes the conditional PDF integrate to one.

questions.question: Inside the conditioning set, the conditional PDF
options: has a different shape from the unconditional PDF
has the same shape as the unconditional PDF, scaled by the constant 1/P(X ∈ A)
questions.correct_answer: has the same shape as the unconditional PDF, scaled by the constant 1/P(X ∈ A)
questions.explanation: Only a vertical rescaling happens; outside the set the conditional PDF is zero.

questions.question: The memorylessness property of the exponential says that, given that no event has occurred by time t, the remaining waiting time
options: is exponential with the same parameter λ, whatever t is
questions.correct_answer: is exponential with the same parameter λ, whatever t is
questions.explanation: The conditional CDF works out to 1 − e^(−λx), independent of the elapsed time t.

questions.question: The conditional expectation given an event A is
questions.explanation: It is the ordinary definition with the conditional PDF in place of the unconditional one.

questions.question: If A_1, …, A_n are disjoint events of positive probability partitioning the sample space, then f_X(x) equals
questions.correct_answer: Σ_i P(A_i) f_{X|A_i}(x)
questions.explanation: This is the total probability theorem written for densities.

questions.question: The total expectation theorem for continuous random variables states that E[X] equals
questions.correct_answer: Σ_i P(A_i) E[X | A_i]
questions.explanation: Multiplying the total probability formula by x and integrating gives the weighted average of conditional means.

questions.question: For the piecewise constant PDF equal to 1/3 on [0,1] and 2/3 on (1,2], the mean is
You arrive uniformly between 7:10 and 7:30 for trains at 7:15 and 7:30. For 0 ≤ y ≤ 5, the waiting-time PDF f_Y(y) is
questions.explanation: Total probability combines the two cases: (1/4)(1/5) + (3/4)(1/15) = 1/10.

questions.question: Two random variables are jointly continuous when
options: each of them separately has a PDF
a nonnegative joint PDF exists whose integral over any region of the plane gives the probability of that region
questions.correct_answer: a nonnegative joint PDF exists whose integral over any region of the plane gives the probability of that region
questions.explanation: Having marginal PDFs is not enough; the pair needs a joint density.

questions.question: The joint PDF f_{X,Y}(a,c) is interpreted as
options: the probability that X = a and Y = c
probability per unit length near a
probability per unit area near the point (a,c)
questions.correct_answer: probability per unit area near the point (a,c)
questions.explanation: For small δ, the probability of the δ-by-δ square at (a,c) is about f_{X,Y}(a,c)·δ².

questions.question: The marginal PDF f_X is obtained from the joint PDF by
options: integrating the joint PDF over y
differentiating the joint PDF with respect to y
dividing the joint PDF by f_Y
evaluating the joint PDF at y = 0
questions.correct_answer: integrating the joint PDF over y
questions.explanation: Letting Y range over the whole line leaves only the dependence on x.

questions.question: For a uniform joint PDF on a set S and any A ⊂ S, P((X,Y) ∈ A) equals
options: area of A divided by area of S
area of A ∩ S divided by area of S
area of S divided by area of A
questions.correct_answer: area of A ∩ S divided by area of S
questions.explanation: A uniform joint PDF makes probability proportional to area, exactly as the discrete uniform law counts outcomes.

questions.question: In Buffon’s needle problem with needle length l and line spacing d (l < d), the probability of intersection is
questions.correct_answer: 2l/(πd)
questions.explanation: Integrating the uniform joint PDF over x ≤ (l/2)sin θ gives 2l/(πd), which also yields an experimental estimate of π.

questions.question: For jointly continuous X and Y and scalars a, b, E[aX + bY] equals
questions.correct_answer: aE[X] + bE[Y]
questions.explanation: Expectation stays linear, whatever the dependence between X and Y.

questions.question: The conditional PDF of X given Y = y is defined, for f_Y(y) > 0, as
questions.correct_answer: f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y)
questions.explanation: It is the discrete formula p_{X|Y} = p_{X,Y}/p_Y with densities in place of masses.

questions.question: For each fixed y with f_Y(y) > 0, the function x ↦ f_{X|Y}(x | y)
options: integrates to 1 over x, so it is a legitimate PDF
questions.correct_answer: integrates to 1 over x, so it is a legitimate PDF
questions.explanation: Dividing by f_Y(y) is exactly the normalization that makes the slice a PDF.

questions.question: The continuous Bayes rule expresses f_{X|Y}(x | y) as
options: f_X(x)f_{Y|X}(y | x) divided by ∫ f_X(t)f_{Y|X}(y | t) dt
questions.correct_answer: f_X(x)f_{Y|X}(y | x) divided by ∫ f_X(t)f_{Y|X}(y | t) dt
questions.explanation: The denominator is f_Y(y), computed by the total probability theorem for densities.

questions.question: When the unobserved quantity X is discrete and the measurement Y is continuous, P(X = x | Y = y) equals
questions.correct_answer: p_X(x)f_{Y|X}(y | x)/f_Y(y)
questions.explanation: Conditioning on {y ≤ Y ≤ y + δ} and letting δ tend to zero cancels δ from numerator and denominator.

questions.question: Two continuous random variables X and Y are independent exactly when
options: f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y) for all x, y
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) + f_Y(y) for all x, y
questions.correct_answer: f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y) for all x, y
questions.explanation: Equivalently f_{X|Y}(x | y) = f_X(x) wherever f_Y(y) > 0: conditioning tells you nothing new.

questions.question: If X and Y are independent, then var(X + Y) equals
questions.correct_answer: var(X) + var(Y)
questions.explanation: Independence also gives E[g(X)h(Y)] = E[g(X)]E[h(Y)] for any functions g and h.

questions.question: The joint PDF is recovered from the joint CDF by
options: differentiating F_{X,Y} with respect to x only
taking the mixed second partial derivative ∂²F_{X,Y}/∂x∂y
questions.correct_answer: taking the mixed second partial derivative ∂²F_{X,Y}/∂x∂y
questions.explanation: Two integrations build the CDF from the PDF, so two differentiations reverse them.

questions.question: For three random variables, the multiplication rule reads
options: f_{X,Y,Z}(x,y,z) = f_{X|Y,Z}(x | y,z) f_{Y|Z}(y | z) f_Z(z)
questions.correct_answer: f_{X,Y,Z}(x,y,z) = f_{X|Y,Z}(x | y,z) f_{Y|Z}(y | z) f_Z(z)
questions.explanation: The product of marginals holds only under independence; the chain rule holds always.

questions.question: The two-step method for finding the PDF of Y = g(X) is
options: compute the CDF F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y), then differentiate it
substitute y for x in f_X
integrate f_X over the range of g
questions.correct_answer: compute the CDF F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y), then differentiate it
questions.explanation: The event {g(X) ≤ y} must first be translated into an event about X.

questions.question: For X uniform on [0,1] and Y = √X, the PDF of Y on [0,1] is
questions.correct_answer: 2y
questions.explanation: F_Y(y) = P(X ≤ y²) = y², and differentiating gives 2y.

questions.question: A 180-mile trip is driven at a speed uniform on [30,60]. The PDF of the duration Y on [3,6] is
questions.correct_answer: 6/y²
questions.explanation: F_Y(y) = 2 − 6/y on that range, and differentiating gives 6/y².

questions.question: For Y = aX + b with a ≠ 0, the PDF of Y is
questions.explanation: The PDF is stretched horizontally by a and scaled vertically by 1/|a| so the area stays one.

questions.question: A linear function of a normal random variable is
options: normal, with mean aμ + b and variance a²σ²
normal, with mean μ and variance σ²
questions.correct_answer: normal, with mean aμ + b and variance a²σ²
questions.explanation: Substituting into the linear-case formula reproduces a normal PDF with those parameters.

questions.question: For strictly monotonic g with inverse h, the PDF of Y = g(X) is
questions.correct_answer: f_X(h(y))·|dh/dy(y)|
questions.explanation: The derivative factor accounts for how the transformation stretches an interval.

questions.question: For X uniform on (0,1] and Y = X², the PDF of Y on (0,1] is
questions.explanation: Here h(y) = √y, so |dh/dy| = 1/(2√y) and f_X(√y) = 1.

questions.question: For independent X and Y uniform on [0,1], the PDF of Z = max{X,Y} on [0,1] is
questions.correct_answer: 2z
questions.explanation: Independence gives F_Z(z) = P(X ≤ z)P(Y ≤ z) = z², and differentiating gives 2z.

questions.question: For independent exponentials X and Y with parameter λ, the PDF of Z = X − Y is
options: (λ/2)e^(−λ|z|), the two-sided exponential or Laplace PDF
questions.correct_answer: (λ/2)e^(−λ|z|), the two-sided exponential or Laplace PDF
questions.explanation: Symmetry between X − Y and Y − X makes the CDF, and hence the PDF, symmetric about zero.

questions.question: Which summary of the special continuous laws is correct?
options: Uniform on [a,b] has variance (b − a)/12, exponential has variance 1/λ, and normal has variance σ
Uniform on [a,b] has variance (b − a)²/12, exponential with parameter λ has variance 1/λ², and normal with parameters μ and σ² has variance σ²
Uniform on [a,b] has variance (b + a)²/12, exponential has variance λ², and normal has variance μ
All three laws have variance equal to their mean
questions.correct_answer: Uniform on [a,b] has variance (b − a)²/12, exponential with parameter λ has variance 1/λ², and normal with parameters μ and σ² has variance σ²
questions.explanation: These are the means and variances derived in the chapter and collected in its summary.
